He wrote The Mind of Primitive Man and taught Alfred Kroeber, Ruth Benedict, and Margaret Mead. Name this Columbia professor considered the father of American anthropology.

One of this man's essays claims the field he was a professor in had the task of "disappearance", while another essay considers the "leafy" nature of leaves. "We Philologists" and "On Truth and Lies in a Non-Moral Sense" were both published posthumously, along with a collection of notes compiled by this man's sister following this philosopher's mental breakdown. Another question asked by this thinker is "Why am I so smart?" in his Ecce Homo. Famous for the doctrine of eternal recurrence and the Apollonian/Dionysian split, as well as the concept of an "Ubermensch", identify this philosopher, author of "The Anti-Christ" and "Beyond Good and Evil".

He broke with another philosopher in his 1937 essay, "The Transcendence of the Ego," in which he distinguished between "intentional" and "incidental" objects. The former are part of human consciousness, which constructs strives to learn more about the outside world, or "The Other." The realization that inanimate objects do not respond to human consciousness underlies his existentialist novel, Nausea, while he proposed the idea that self- consciousness has a "masochistic desire". For ten pionts, name this French philosopher and author of Existentialism is a Humanism as well as Being and Nothingness.

Some of the lesser known works written by this philosopher include The Principle of Ground and The Self-Assertion of the German University, and scholars agree that his inaugural address as head of Freiburg constituted an important Kehre. He often lectured on the necessity of the spirit of the Volk, and in one of his works, he argued that only through acknowledgement of existential angst can one achieve rapport with the Being. Another important work by this author is What Is Metaphysics?, and a third is Kant and the Problem of Metaphysics. Identify this Nazi charlatan and German philosopher, the author of Being and Time.

In one of this philosopher's works, he advocates a Galilean cosmology, and in the same work, he wrote about the study of light refraction in Dioptrics. One thing named for this philosopher consists of the admonitions to admit as true only what was so perfectly clear and distinct that it was indubitable, and to make such accurate enumerations of the steps of reasoning so as to be certain of having omitted nothing, known as his method of doubt, and which can be found in Meditations on First Philosophy. Identify this philosopher, whose best known for his work Discourse on Method and the statement of existence "Cogito ergo sum".

A strong influence on Fichte's Doctrine of Science, this work claims that the form of freedom can be experienced through the force of moral law, but that two other concepts have been reduced to "postulates of reason." The shorter of two works utilizing the familiar structure of a "Doctrine of Elements" followed by a "Methodology," this work was meant as a demonstrative response to the charge that undermining the synthetic a priori removes the possibility of morality. The application of the principles of this work can be found in Die Metaphysik der Sitten, or The Metaphysics of Morals, since it deals with ethics in terms of a required practical component of knowledge. Name this work by Immanuel Kant, the second of his major critiques.

The objects of dialectic in this work are the Thebans Simmias and Cebes, the latter of whom initiates a long discussion of suicide to clarify the mandate "come after me if [you] be a wise man." Ending with an order to give a cock to Asclepius, this philosophical work sees the positing and eventual dismissal of the model of the lyre, the harmony from which dissipates when it is broken. The final argument about the central concept in this work is that it participates in the Form of Life and, as such, cannot by definition die. Name this Platonic dialogue chiefly notable for Socrates' doctrine of the immortality of the soul.

One of the ideas advanced in this book divides characteristics into either primary or secondary, the first of which is innate to an object, and the second of which is within the observer. Another idea in this work states that all objects have innate substance. Its second book states that "all ideas come from sensation or reflection", which underscores its creator's belief that no knowledge is innate. A reaction to rationalist thinking, it carefully examines the concept of identity, and states that man knows of three substances: God, finite intelligences, and bodies. Name this 1690 essay by John Locke.

In the third book of this work, the author comes to the conclusion that tragedy is the summit of poetry, and that we can observe in nature the war of one of the title concepts with itself. In this book, the author defines the beauty of an object as what occurs when it realizes one of the title concepts. In the last book, the author posits that the idea of life is tragic, and examines the denial of the will to live. One of the title concepts in this work is defined as "a striving, yearning force that takes various forms according to its inclinations", and this work posits that by losing oneself in objects, one can realize the truth of the title concept. Identify this pessimistic philosophical text, the seminal work by Arthur Schopenhauer.
The World as Will and Idea

Glenn Reeder argued against John Harvey's 1981 article claiming that this was a misnomer, and Joseph Forgas showed that it is less severe in people in bad moods. Evidence for this comes from a 1977 paper in which neutral observers rated people who asked difficult questions more knowledgeable than their counterparts who could not answer them, and from a 1967 paper by Jones and Harris in which people listening to a speech about Castro identified the speaker's true beliefs as consistent with the speech. For ten points name this common mistake, discovered by Lee Ross, in which people underestimate the effect of situational factors and overestimate the effect of internal factors on one's behavior.

In one of this philosopher's works, he argues against a charge of treason by Odyssues in the Defense of Palamedes. In another work, via proof by exhaustion, he exculpates a different major figure of the Trojan War; that is his Encomium of Helen. In addition to Pyrhho, this philosopher's work is transmitted through Sextus Empiricus, who wrote of the metaphysical solipsism presented in this man's On Non-Existence. His eponymous Platonic dialogue features Polus and Callicles, who orders Socrates to debate himself. Name this Greek, whose sophism, like that of Protagoras, is contrasted with Socratic philosophy.

His aesthetic approach was based on Humbert de Superville's Essay on the Unmistakable Signs of Art and the integrationist approach of David Sutter. His final grand-scale work was Les Poseuses, which he followed with a painting whose subject he was secretly involved with, Jeune Femme se Poudrant. Another painting, Une Baignade, Asnières, demonstrates his technique of using tiny brushstrokes which become incoherent at a close distance. Name this pointillist who depicted a pet monkey and some women with parasols in Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.

This philosopher's most famous argument was modified by the "envy test" of Ronald Dworkin. One of his works uses the term "consultation hierarchies" to refer to benign non-democracies, while he outlines an "overlapping consensus" of the private sphere in his work Political Liberalism. He applied his "original position" argument to international relations in 1999's The Law of Peoples, while his most famous work discusses the "difference principle" and "fairness principle," and was criticized by Robert Nozick in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. FTP, name this American political philosopher who introduced the "veil of ignorance" in 1971's A Theory of Justice.

He created the NF system of set theory and, with Hilary Putnam, made an "indispensability argument" for the reality of mathematical entities. He advocated looking to the limits of a formal language in order to determine the "ontological commitments" of any statement in that language in his The Ways of Paradox and Ontological Relativity, and he identified logical reductionism and the analytic/synthetic distinction as the titular fallacies of another work. Name this American analytic philosopher, the author of Word and Object and "Two Dogmas of Empiricism."

He posited a "law of conservation of difficulty," saying that simpler fields develop more obscurantist vocabularies, in his essay "Postmodernism Disrobed." His last book denounces "tremulous Martin Luther King impersonations" and describes one subject as "comparable to the smallpox virus but harder to eradicate." One of his earliest forays into metaphysics was titled in reference to a William Paley argument, and he later argued that children should not be taught metaphysical beliefs and advocated the term "Bright" to describe those who reject all superstition. Name this author of The Blind Watchmaker and The God Delusion, a biologist and evangelizing atheist.

This philosopher attacked Leibniz's categorization of logical operations in The False Subtlety of the Four Syllogistic Figures. This person's idea of the "inner being" was the subject of Michael Foucalt's doctoral dissertation. Following Grotius, he called for a ban on assassination, an end to standing armies, and the clarification of treaties to accomplish the title goal of Perpetual Peace, and he also divided representation between intuitions and concepts, and judgments between analytic and synthetic. Name this author of The Metaphysics of Morals and Critique of Pure Reason, which explains the categorical imperative.

This thinker defined modernity as the loss of the private world due to a two-stage process of "world-alienation" and "earth-alienation" in Between Past and Future. This philosopher's threefold classifications include labor, work, and action, in The Human Condition and thinking, willing, and judging in The Life of the Mind. She defined the title form of government as "the inversion of politics" in On Totalitarianism, and argued that conscience should be a byproduct of thinking and one should consider human consequences in Eichmann in Jerusalem. Name this philosopher who discussed the "banality of evil."

As a philosopher, his most important works are 'Concerning Genera and Species,' which deals with logic and dialectic, and 'Know Thyself,' an ethical treatise. His best-selling book, however, is the autobiographical 'History of My Calamities,' which tells of how his brother-in-law broke into his room one night and made him a eunuch. FTP, name this castrated 12th-century French theologian and lover of Heloise.

His philosophical mentor and his father cooperated to teach him mathematics at age three, logic and political economy by age twelve. He suffered a nervous breakdown at age 21 from which he emerged with a new appreciation for the emotional side of experience. Despite his protestations to the contrary, some of the views expressed in his treatises on utilitarianism differed from those of his mentor. FTP, name the philospher.

A graduate of Trinity College and later a deacon, librarian, and lecturer there, this Anglo-Irish bishop of Cloyne is better known for philosophical works such as 1709's 'Toward A New Theory Of Vision.' His philosophy was Locke-influenced Empiricism, as he laid out in 1713's 'Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonius.' FTP identify this idealist and immaterialist philosopher, whose credo was 'To be is to be perceived.'

A 1784 essay on this concept claims that only the freedom to use reason publically in all matters is necessary for this to happen. That essay, whose title asks the question, "What is [this concept]" claims that it is "man's emergence from his self-imposed immaturity." That essay on this concept was a response to a reverend's question from a 1783 German periodical in Berlin. Proposing that the age of this concept is the "age of Frederick," and that the motto of this concept is "Have the courage to use your own understanding," FTP name this concept articulated by Immanuel Kant, a period of intellectual awakening in Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.

First suggested by Aristotle in his De Anima, a contemporary work titled after this concept claims that modern science has challenged this concept along with the "noble savage" and "the ghost in the machine," and was written by Steven Pinker. In the Platonic dialogue Meno, the slave boy "recalling" the Pythagorean Theorem from prompting by Socrates can be seen as a contradiction to this epistemological concept. Provide this epistemological term, which suggests that individuals are born without any innate knowledge or memories, formulated by John Locke with a Latin term meaning "blank slate."

The Kyriai Doxai, or "Principal Doctrines," is a collection of forty aphorisms by this thinker which were preserved by Diogenes Laertius. His house near Athens on the road from Dipylos featured a secluded garden which gave its name to the community of like-minded followers who met with him there. He extolled the importance of ataraxia, or "freedom from disturbance," an idea propounded by his later follower Lucretius, which could be attained by limiting desire but by satisfying necessities. FTP name this Hellenistic philosopher whose namesake school equates pleasure with the good.

One work by this author attempts to defend the truth of divine revelation against such Freethinkers as the Earl of Shaftesbury; titled with the name of a Greek sophist, it is subtitled The Minute Philosopher. In addition to writing Alciphron, this author also rejected Newtonian mechanics in De Motu. He critiques materialist ontologies and empiricist epistemologies in a work that presents his so-called "master argument," regarding conceivability in which one of the interlocutors is meant to represent John Locke. Claiming "to be is to be perceived," FTP name this Anglo-Irish immaterialist philosopher and fan of tar-water, author of Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous.

One essay that critiques traditional understandings of this concept uses a series of propositions about "Jones owning a Ford" and whether Brown lives in Boston, Barcelona, or Brest-Litovsk to reject Chisolm's and Ayer's formulation of this concept. That essay by Edmund Gettier critiques a theory of this concept first put forth in the Socratic dialogue the Theatetus. Foucault suggests that this concept reproduces power and vice-versa, and Quine rejected the distinction between the analytic and synthetic forms of this concept. Coined by James Frederick Fourier, the name of the study of this concept is epistemology. FTP name this concept whose definition as "justified true belief" is in doubt.

The title of a 1916 work which claims that nations ought to have a balance between lions and foxes in the elite class, written by Vilfredo Pareto, pairs this concept with Society. Betrand Russell's article "On Denoting" and Alan Turing's article "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" both appeared in a journal titled this. A work that discusses the development of higher psychological processes by Lev Vygotsky is titled [this concept] in Society. The inverted spectrum and explanatory gap arguments are used to hypothesize the existence of qualia in order explain the possible dichotomy between this concept and the body, a dichotomy conceptualized in the 17th century by Rene Descartes. FTP name this aspect of intellect and consciousness that may or may not be reduced to states of the brain.

The namesake "club" of this group of thinkers included George Putnam, William Henry Channing, and George Ripley, all of whom rejected the emphasis on sense data as the basis of cognition. Influenced by the mysticism of Swedenborg, its adherents argued against the emphasis on historicity in Christianity, particularly in the church to which most of the belonged, the Unitarian Church. Considered by some to have begun with the 1836 publication of the essay "Nature," FTP what is this philosophical tendency shared by Margaret Fuller, Orestes Brownson, and, most particularly, Ralph Waldo Emerson?

This man gave a lecture about psychology claiming that "Introspection forms no essential part of its methods." His 1928 work Psychological Care of the Infant and Child is no longer considered a standard text, and ironically he himself later claimed he didn't know enough to write it. With his assistant Rosalie Raynor, this man conducted an experiment in which he struck a metal pipe with a hammer to scare an infant into associating that fear with a pet rat. Resulting in the child fearing all white fluffy things. FTP name this author of the book named for his psychological beliefs, Behaviorism.

This author suggested that there is no other road to truth except through the "brook of fire," referring to this philosopher's admiration of the writings of Ludwig Feuerbach. This author satirizes Bastiat's theory of credit as an "utter poverty of ideas under a cover of formal logic" in his Grundrisse. In addition to writing Notes on James Mill and The Civil War in France, this theorist in perhaps his most famous work claims that the constant revolutionizing of production leads to a constant disturbance of social conditions thus "all that is solid melts into air, [and] all that is holy is profaned." Also the author of the Critique of the Gotha Program, that quote comes from a work co-written by Friedrich Engels and warns of a specter haunting Europe. FTP name this German philosopher who discussed the class struggle between bourgeoisie and the proletariat in the Communist Manifesto.

This work's third and fourth sections attempt to define thought, while a statement in the fifth posits that bit patterns map onto sentences. Its succinct style is modeled on Frege's. The final section of this work, placed directly after a reference to Schopenhauer's ladder analogy, is proposition seven, is the only proposition with no sub-statements, which claims "What we cannot speak of we must pass over in silence." what is this logical-positivist tome, the only book-length work of Ludwig Wittgenstein?

This author of Three Essays on Religion wrote a treatise which explains the different sensations produced by drunkenly breaking dishware versus listening to classical music. Author of A System of Logic, he produced a political work which declares the idea of truth always triumphing a "pleasant falsehood" and establishes the "harm principle." In another of his essays, he decries the conversion of a "physical fact" into a "legal right" and bemoans the survival of marriage as a form of legalized slavery, advocating the equality of the sexes. Name this author of Utilitarianism, On Liberty, and The Subjection of Women.

Aristotle describes this thinker as older than Empedocles, but "after him in works." He thought that heavenly bodies were pieces of Earth that had broken off and were ignited from rotation, which got him exiled from Athens. Apparently an adherent of Anaximines' thought, he postulated a plurality of "seeds," which were the smallest independent elements out of which everything was made, proceeding from the nous. Identify this pre-Socratic philosopher from Clazomenae, author of "On Nature."

This work's fifth chapter examines the rational, empirical, and ethical shapes of reason, while the seventh chapter discusses natural religion and examines the interplay between the artist and his age. This work begins with an explication of sensory, perceptual, and understanding consciousness, while its fourth chapter examines the master and slave consciousness. With a last chapter dedicated to "Absolute Knowing," identify this work that traces the development of the title thought-based entity through the dialectic, a work of Georg Willhelm Hegel.

During his stay in Dresden, he met Karl Krause who introduced him to pantheism, an idea that he would later incorporate into his own work. His doctoral thesis, The Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason, introduced his arguments against German idealists such as Schelling and Hegel. His later works include the essays On the Freedom of the Human Will and On the Basis of Morality and the set of philosophical reflections, Parerga und Paralipomena. Identify this pessimistic German philosopher and author of The World as Will and Representation.

This work's Exordium depicts an event in four different scenarios and the main section, Problemata, poses such questions as "Is there a Teleological Suspension of the Ethical?" about that event. Its title refers to Philippians, but it compares the Knight of Infinite Resignation to the Knight of Faith using a story from Genesis. Originally published under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio, its theme has also been interpreted as an allegory for the author's failed engagement to Regine Olsen. Examining Abraham's faith when commanded to sacrifice Isaac, what is this 1843 work by Søren Kierkegaard?

French philosopher Bernard Stiegler was heavily influenced by this philosopher, and interpreted his work in a work about a "Fault of Epimetheus." Victor Farias criticized this philosopher for his political views, and this philosopher's thought was said to undergo a "turn" or "die Kehre." His lectures include one on "Hölderlin's Hymn: The Ister." Another of his works was intended to have a second part about the "destruktion" of the history of philosophy, and the first part of that work introduced the being for whom being is in question, dasein. Name this German philosopher who wrote Being and Time.

The last paragraph of this book describes sub specie aeternitatis, and the author describes how "the perspective of eternity is not a perspective from a certain place beyond the world." This work claims that actors will adopt a "maximin" strategy and strive for "primary social goods" in theorizing a counterpart to Hobbes's "state of nature" that it dubs the "original position." This book describes two sub-ideas of its main theme, the Principle of Equal, and the Difference Principle, and was refuted in Robert Nozzick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Name this work that describes "a veil of ignorance," a 1971 work by John Rawls.

This man argued in a thought experiment that private objects are "irrelevant," an idea reinterpreted upon in Saul Kripke's work about this man "On Rules and Private Language." He introduced the concept of "familial relations" in a work that derided philosophy as a series of language games, and he attempted to set out a logically perfect language in another work that begins "The world is everything that is the case" and ends by claiming that what we cannot speak of, we must pass over in silence. Name this Austrian philosopher, author of The Blue and Brown Books, Philosophical Investigations and Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus.

This designer of the Chresthomatic Day School used the penname Gamliel Smith to write a paper questioning the authority of a Biblical figure, "Not Paul but Jesus." He published his first work "A Fragment on Government" in response to William Blackstone's love of the "rule of law." This philosopher sent Adam Smith a letter arguing for free lending of money at interest, included in his Defense of Usury, and he introduced the central concept of his philosophy in Introduction to Principles of Morals. Name this theorizer of the Panopticon and founder of utilitarianism.

This man's conflicts with other philosophers include a critique of J.J. Gibson's "ecological psychology," written with Zenon Pylyshyn, and a long debate with Jaegwon Kim regarding this man's theory of multiple realizability. He attempts to combine Davidson's Swamp-Man and Putnam's Twin-Earth in an appendix to his work, The Elm and the Expert, though his most famous work was expanded on by Steven Pinker in How the Mind Works, a book this man notably disliked and responded to with his own work, The Mind Doesn't Work That Way. FTP, name this analytic philosopher who argued for a difference between mental and public languages in The Language of Thought, and developed a theory of brain organization in Modularity of the Mind.

This theory is paired with functionalism in a 1985 article by John McDowell, which looks at Brian Loar's argument against it. Ted Honderich authored a paper on the "argument for" it, writing that it cannot survive the charge of epiphenomalism, while another paper asks whether "supervenience" can save this theory, and was written by Jaegwon Kim. It assumes the "Principle of the Nomological Character of Causality" and applies its formulator's "principle of charity," also central to his method of radical interpretation. It posits the creation of "token-identities" through the impossibility of type-identities. First introduced in a paper entitled "Mental Events," it claims that those mental events are identical to certain physical events but cannot be reduced to them by strict laws. FTP, name this mind-body theory formulated by Donald Davidson.

At one point, this work quotes Cardinal de Retz as saying that great dangers have their charms, because there is some glory to be got even when we miscarry. In an oft-cited passage, the author writes that a certain "spirit of system" and a "love of art and contrivance" can cause us to value the means more than the end, in a chapter entitled "Of the beauty which the appearance of Utility bestows upon the productions of art." The second part discusses the "merit and demerit" of actions as their "good or ill desert," while earlier the author claims that "imaginary change of situation" is the main characteristic of sympathy. More famously, this work claims that the "man within the breast" is the abstract and ideal spectator who must be awakened and put in mind of his duty by the real spectator. Inspired by the author's teacher Frances Hutcheson, FTP, name this ethical treatise, the first major work by Adam Smith.

Thomas Hall and Christopher Chase-Dunn compared different examples of these entities in Rise and Demise. Janet Abu-Lughod argued that one of these entities emerged in the thirteenth century in her book Before European Hegemony. Andre Gunder Frank's book ReOrient argues for a single one of these centered in China and lasting the last five thousand years. Theories about these entities divide countries into core, semi-peripheral, and peripheral zones. Dependency theorists argue that, in the modern one of these, the wealthy core countries exploit the poorer periphery. One of his most important works contains sections such as "Means and Ends" and "Conflicting Panaceas;" those sections discuss distinctions between subjective, objective, and instrumental versions of the title concept, with emphasis on how the Nazis applied it. Along with another writer, this author of The Authoritarian State and The Eclipse of Reason wrote a work which contained two Excurses on Odysseus and Juliette and a discussion of anti-Semitism, in addition to an exposition of what he called the "culture industry."
